title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 3: Can the Senate Stop a GMA Holdover?
keywords: Can the Senate Stop a GMA Holdover?
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6) -- CJP's February 7, 2010 Inquirer column examining whether the Senate can block a Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo 'holdover' presidency if a partial failure of elections leaves the country with no proclaimed successors when all top officials' terms end on June 30, 2010

The readers' proposed fix -- electing a Senate president whose term runs to 2013 to act as president -- and why it 'is not [that simple],' since it rests on the contested premise that the Senate is a 'continuing body'

The continuing-body problem -- under earlier Constitutions a staggered Senate always left a 16-member majority in office, but under the present charter only 12 of 24 remain after an election, so GMA's partisans could argue the Senate has 'ceased to be a continuing body,' a question only the Supreme Court can settle

The Court angle and the automation risks -- why a contested holdover made a 'credible' Court essential (bearing on the rushed JBC nominations during the appointment ban), and why eight months was too little to perfect a nationwide PCOS system, raising the odds of a 'no-proc' gridlock
sub_topics: The scenario: CJP had argued that a failed election in 15 percent of the country could give GMA 'the opportunity to become a holdover president,' because the constitutional successors -- VP Noli de Castro, Senate President Enrile, and Speaker Nograles -- would, like her, 'end their terms... on June 30, 2010'
The readers' fix: the 'near unanimous' reader reaction was to elect a Senate president whose term runs to 2013, who could then act as president -- but CJP cautions the solution 'is not' simple

The continuing-body premise: the fix assumes the Senate is a 'continuing body' whose officers stay on between adjournments, a notion derived from earlier Constitutions that staggered 24 senators 'in batches of eight every two years,' always leaving 16 in office

Why it may fail now: under the present Constitution '12 of the 24 Senators are elected every three years,' so only 12 -- 'who do not constitute a majority' -- remain, letting GMA's partisans argue the Senate is no longer continuing and its new head cannot become acting president

Who decides: the continuity question would fall to the Supreme Court -- and the prospect that the Court would decide the holdover issue, CJP notes, 'propelled the presidential allies' to push the JBC to submit Chief Justice nominees even before CJ Puno's May 17 retirement, in apparent violation of the March 11-June 30 appointment ban

The 'credible SC' point: the Palace had not categorically said it would appoint within the banned period (saying only it would do 'what the national interest requires'), which CJP reads as GMA 'keeping her options open' -- since as a holdover she could name the Chief Justice after June 30, and a 'non-controversial Court' would be needed to make a holdover publicly acceptable

Computerization needs time: even the long-running ATM and credit-card systems took years to perfect, yet serve far fewer users than the 82,200 PCOS machines and 47 million voters; field-test transmissions took 'several hours' (against a credit card's seconds), and even the Supreme Court's own decade-old computerization remained incomplete -- so eight months could not suffice

The 'no-proc' odds: with 'many other dangers' (ballot-printing delays, PCOS miscalibration, misdelivery, transmission glitches, hacking, weak training, ballot theft) and surveys showing a 'neck-and-neck race,' a no-proclamation gridlock could arise even from glitches in as little as five percent of the votes -- about two million ballots -- so 'the closer the presidential race is, the more [likely] holdover becomes'

stances.claim: Electing a 2013-term Senate president to act as president is not a clean fix, because under the present Constitution only 12 senators remain after an election -- not a majority -- so GMA's partisans could argue the Senate is no longer a 'continuing body' and its new head cannot act as president.

stances.claim: Because the Supreme Court would decide the holdover question, a 'credible' and 'non-controversial' Court is essential -- which is why the rushed JBC nominations during the appointment ban (to seat a Chief Justice before Puno's retirement) would 'politicize the SC' and were being kept as an open option.

stances.claim: Eight months could not perfect a nationwide PCOS system -- ATMs, credit cards and even the SC's own computerization took years -- so 'many dangers' make a 'no-proc' gridlock plausible even from five percent glitched votes, and the closer the race, the more likely a holdover.
stances.rhetorical_move: analogy-and-risk inventory: using familiar tech timelines to puncture the rushed rollout

notable_anecdotes: 82,200 vs. a few thousand: CJP contrasts the 82,200 PCOS machines (for 47 million voters) with the far fewer, urban-only ATMs that still 'took many years to install and to perfect.'
Five seconds, not hours: he relays a self-confessed 'geek' reader's point that a credit-card authorization takes seconds, while PCOS field-test transmissions took 'several hours.'
The Court's own unfinished system: he notes the Supreme Court's computerization, begun a decade earlier under CJ Davide, 'is still incomplete' -- proof that such systems can't be rushed.
Two million ballots: he warns a 'no-proc' could arise from glitches in just five percent of votes -- about two million ballots -- enough to stall a close race into a holdover.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's February 7, 2010 Inquirer column, asks whether the Senate can stop a Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo 'holdover' presidency. He had argued that a failed election in 15 percent of the country could let GMA hold over, since the constitutional successors -- VP de Castro, Senate President Enrile, and Speaker Nograles -- would all 'end their terms... on June 30, 2010.' Readers near-unanimously proposed electing a Senate president whose term runs to 2013 to act as president, but CJP warns 'it is not' that simple: the fix assumes the Senate is a 'continuing body,' a notion rooted in earlier Constitutions that staggered 24 senators 'eight every two years' (leaving 16 in office), whereas under the present charter only 12 remain after an election -- 'who do not constitute a majority' -- so GMA's partisans could argue the Senate has 'ceased to be a continuing body.' That question would fall to the Supreme Court, and CJP reads the rushed JBC push to name a Chief Justice before Puno's May 17 retirement (during the March 11-June 30 appointment ban) as an attempt to control the holdover ruling -- though the Palace kept it an 'option,' since a 'credible' and 'non-controversial' Court would be needed to make any holdover publicly acceptable. He then warns that eight months could not perfect a nationwide PCOS system: ATMs, credit cards and even the Court's own decade-old computerization took years; PCOS field-test transmissions ran 'several hours' against a credit card's seconds; and with 82,200 machines, 47 million voters, and 'many other dangers' (printing delays, miscalibration, misdelivery, hacking, weak training), a 'no-proc' gridlock could arise from glitches in just five percent of votes -- about two million ballots. His conclusion: 'the closer the presidential race is, the more [likely] holdover becomes.'
